No failure path may be silent. Four exist, and each gets a way of being seen.

**A session that will not convert.** Today it is skipped with `continue` and
simply never appears — the only sign is a missing row nobody counts. Instead
every failure is recorded in `.build-errors.json` as session id, source path,
error and time, and the index renders a banner at the top listing them. A
session you cannot see is reported rather than absent.

**A build that partly failed.** `build.sh` exits non-zero and prints each
failure. The index still builds from what succeeded, so a single bad transcript
cannot cost you the other sixty-eight — but the banner says so.

**A hook that failed.** Hook output goes into the transcript where it is easy to
miss, so the archiving hook writes its own failures to the same
`.build-errors.json`. A session that failed to archive at exit is then reported
the next time you open the index, which is when you would care.

**A page that is stale.** Each page records the mtime of the source it was built
from. If the source is newer, the page says so in its header and the index marks
the row, rather than quietly showing an old conversation.

new:
## Diffs

`render_diff` currently uses `difflib.unified_diff`. The viewer needs an
equivalent, and this is the part most likely to go wrong quietly: a diff
algorithm produces plausible output for any input, so a bad alignment does not
crash, it just attributes changes to the wrong lines.

**An earlier draft of this spec had the acceptance criterion wrong.** It said
the new diff must "agree line for line" with `difflib`. That is not a sound
test. `difflib` is `SequenceMatcher` — Ratcliff/Obershelp with an autojunk
heuristic — not Myers. Two different, equally correct diffs of the same pair can
align differently. Demonstrated on `one two three four` → `one three two four`,
`difflib` moves `three` up while a Myers implementation may just as correctly
move `two` down. Holding a correct implementation to that criterion would
produce failures that are not bugs, and invite "fixing" it until it is wrong.

The criterion is instead a property of the diff itself:

> **Applying the diff to `old_string` must reproduce `new_string` exactly.**

This is engine-independent, exhaustively checkable, and true of any correct
diff regardless of alignment. The corpus is every `Edit` ever made across the
sessions on disk — **303 real edits** — and the property has already been
verified to hold on all 303 for the current implementation, so it is known to
be a criterion the tool can meet rather than an aspiration.

Alignment quality is then a separate, weaker check: the number of changed lines
the new implementation produces must not exceed `difflib`'s by more than a small
margin on the same corpus. A diff can be correct but noisy; this catches that
without demanding identity.

**Fallback if quality proves poor.** The `Edit` tool gives us `old_string` and
`new_string` directly, so a diff is a presentation choice, not a necessity. If
a hand-written diff cannot be made both correct and tidy, the viewer renders
before-and-after blocks instead: less elegant, zero algorithmic risk, and still
answers "what changed". This is the escape hatch that keeps the diff off the
critical path of the whole migration.

# claude-html

Turn your Claude Code sessions into static HTML you can read, search and
resume — no server, no database, no dependencies to install.

Two earlier versions of this needed a stack to run (Laravel + MySQL, then
Express). This one writes plain files. You open them with a double click.

Pages are written wherever you tell the installer to put them; the examples
below use its default, `~/Sites/claude-html`.

```
<your pages directory>/
├── index.html          every session, searchable
├── <session-id>.html   one page per session
├── search-index.js     full text of every message
└── resume/             double-clickable launchers, one per session
```

## What you get

**An index of every session** — date, project, the title Claude gave the
conversation, and how many prompts you actually typed. A filter box narrows the
list as you type.

**Full-text search across every conversation.** Your prompts, Claude's replies
and its thinking, from all sessions at once. Results show a snippet with your
terms highlighted and link to the exact message, which the page scrolls to and
highlights. Multiple words must all appear in the same message; `"quoted text"`
matches as a phrase.

**Readable session pages.** Tool calls are labelled rather than dumped as JSON.
Every `Edit` becomes a real unified diff. Commands, diffs and file writes show
without a click; what a call returned stays folded. Thinking is kept, collapsed.
Sub-agent turns are marked as such instead of being mixed into your own.

**A way back in.** Every page carries its `claude --resume` command, and
`resume/` holds a `.command` launcher per session — double-click it in Finder
and the session reopens in Terminal, in the right directory.

**Sessions that outlive the transcripts.** Claude Code deletes raw transcripts
after `cleanupPeriodDays`. A hook archives each one as it ends, so the record
survives.

## Requirements

- macOS or Linux (the `.command` launchers are macOS-only; everything else is
  portable)
- Python 3.9+ — standard library only, nothing to `pip install`
- `jq`, for the archiving hook only (`brew install jq`)
- Claude Code

The pages themselves need nothing at all — they are static files.

## Install

```bash
git clone <this-repo> ~/claude-html
cd ~/claude-html
./install.sh
```

It asks two questions — where your projects live and where the pages should go
— then does the rest: puts `claude-html` on your `PATH`, adds the hooks that
archive each session, keeps raw transcripts from being deleted after 30 days,
and builds your pages once.

Answer nothing and it uses `~/Sites` and `~/Sites/claude-html`. To skip the
questions entirely:

```bash
./install.sh --root ~/code
```

Running it again is safe: it changes nothing already set up, and never
overwrites a setting you chose yourself. To undo it, `./install.sh --uninstall`
— which removes the command and the hooks, and leaves your pages and archives
alone.

### What it changed

- `~/.claude/claude-html.conf` — the two directories you chose
- `~/.claude/settings.json` — hooks for `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact`, so
  sessions are archived before Claude Code deletes them, plus
  `cleanupPeriodDays: 3650` if you had not set it yourself
- a `claude-html` symlink in `~/.local/bin` or `/usr/local/bin`

Archives go to `<project>/.claude/.claude-conversations/`, beside the code they
belong to.

### Doing it by hand

If you would rather not run a script, the whole of it is: make the scripts
executable, symlink `claude-html` onto your `PATH`, and add those two hooks to
`settings.json`. Read `install.sh` — it is short, and does nothing else.

### Changing your mind later

Edit `~/.claude/claude-html.conf`, or set either variable in the environment,
which wins over the file:

| Variable            | Default              | Meaning                     |
| ------------------- | -------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `CLAUDE_HTML_ROOT`  | `~/Sites`            | Where your projects live    |
| `CLAUDE_HTML_OUT`   | `$ROOT/claude-html`  | Where the pages are written |

Only sessions started inside the root are archived, which keeps unrelated work
out of your history.

## Usage

```bash
claude-html                 # build changed sessions, open the index
claude-html --force         # rebuild everything
claude-html <session-id>    # rebuild one session
```

Sessions whose source has not changed are skipped, so a rebuild after a day's
work takes a fraction of a second rather than seconds.

## How it works

Sessions come from two places, newest first:

| Source     | Path                                            | Life                   |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| transcript | `~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<id>.jsonl`           | until `cleanupPeriodDays` |
| archive    | `<project>/.claude/.claude-conversations/*.json`| permanent              |

Where both exist the transcript wins, since it carries more.

A few decisions worth knowing about:

**The working directory is read from inside the transcript, not from its
directory name.** Claude encodes `/` as `-` in that name, so a project whose own
name contains a hyphen decodes to a path that does not exist.

**Old archives have their roles inferred.** Early versions of the archiver filed
tool output as something the user said, which made a 49-prompt session read as
1,125. Turn order gives them back: a tool result can only follow the assistant
turn that called the tool. Pages built this way say `archive (inferred)` rather
than implying the roles were recorded.

**Older archives kept a tool's name but not its arguments.** Those cannot be
recovered, but the output of each call can be matched back to it, so a `Read`
shows the file it read and a `Bash` its output.

**Tool output is not indexed for search.** It is nearly half the corpus and a
match inside a command dump is rarely the one you wanted.

**The search index loads on your first keystroke, as a script tag.** These pages
are opened by double click, and browsers block `fetch` against `file://` URLs.

## Tests

```bash
cd <where you cloned it>
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
```

No test framework to install. They cover the parsing and rendering decisions
above, including the ones that exist because something was once wrong.

## Privacy

Everything stays on your machine. Nothing is uploaded, and the pages make no
network requests — no fonts, no analytics, no CDN.

Your conversations are in these files in full, including anything you pasted
into them. The pages directory is deliberately not a git repository: it is
generated output, rebuildable at any time, and not something to publish by
accident. If you point a web server at it, put it behind auth.
